title: Zebra Stripes Were Never About Camouflage
description:
The popular explanation for zebra stripes -- camouflage from lions -- has actually been tested and doesn't hold up. Researchers have since found the real reason, and it has nothing to do with predators.

#shorts #sciencefacts #zebra #didyouknow
sources: UCLA Newsroom's "Why do zebras have stripes?"
National Geographic's coverage of the 2018 Scientific Reports temperature study
Egri et al., Journal of Experimental Biology (2012), "Polarotactic tabanids find striped patterns... least attractive"
PMC/NCBI coverage of horsefly polarotaxis and zebra stripe research

scenes.text: You've probably heard that zebras have stripes for camouflage, to confuse lions during a chase. Scientists actually tested that idea, and it doesn't hold up.
Researchers compared striping patterns against real lion attack data and found no meaningful link at all. Lions catch striped zebras about as easily as anything else.
A separate theory, that the stripes cool zebras down by creating tiny air currents, was also directly tested in 2018. It didn't hold up either.
The explanation with the strongest evidence is almost absurdly small: biting flies. Horseflies are drawn to polarized light bouncing off a smooth, solid-colored coat.

In a 2012 study, striped models attracted far fewer flies than solid black, brown, or grey ones -- the alternating stripes break up that polarized reflection, making zebras a much harder target to land on.
That matters more than it sounds. These flies spread serious diseases, so avoiding them is a real survival advantage, not a small one.
Did you grow up believing the camouflage explanation too?
